## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{100}{0}{0}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why is a completed agent run not enough evidence to justify a release?_

An agent that finishes a run has produced an artifact and a claim, not a verdict. The claim can be wrong in ways the run never reveals. A repair can pass because the agent weakened the test that would have caught it, a report can describe checks nobody ran, and a success can fail to recur when the same task arrives again. Every later decision about an agentic system rests on verdicts of this kind. Releasing a new configuration, choosing which trajectories become training data, and pricing the cost of an accepted task all assume that someone knows which runs actually met their requirements and how much that knowledge can be trusted. Taking the question seriously changes what counts as a result. Acceptance becomes a stated contract rather than an impression, a stochastic system is compared with its predecessor on the same tasks with its uncertainty reported, and an unfinished or unobservable outcome stays visible instead of quietly becoming a pass. Evaluation therefore sits between the runtime that executes trajectories and every process that ships them or learns from them. When it is loose, its errors reach both, and a lower reported cost can reflect nothing more than a laxer acceptance rule. Through the H·S·A lens, evaluation audits each exposure after the fact, checking the state a result rests on, the resources spent across its horizon, and the authority exercised along the way.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Construct a task acceptance contract that credits a trial only on evidence and keeps pending and unknown verdicts in the count
- Design comparable trials that hold task fixtures, reset conditions, and the task sample fixed across compared configurations
- Select and calibrate outcome checks and human or model judges by measuring false acceptance against independent assessment
- Calculate uncertainty for an acceptance rate and a paired difference, using the task rather than the run as the sampling unit
- Compare repeated-run consistency, candidate availability, and cost per accepted task under the deployed selection policy
- Design trace retention policies that keep rare failures and unbiased failure rates within a storage budget
- Design staged releases that size canary exposure with sequential stopping rules and independent hard tripwires
- Synthesize trials, paired comparisons, and release conditions into an evaluation record that justifies a scoped decision

:::

## The Evaluation Problem {#sec-vol3-evaluation-problem}

For the repair agent (\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}), the connection-pool repair has reached the end of its runtime story. The runtime can reconstruct candidate `ws_r18`, retain its unresolved test operation, and account for a temporary integration-test environment. A targeted test result supports that candidate and that check, and a completed cleanup supports the cleanup postcondition. Whether the whole repair meets its requirements is a separate question, which @sec-vol3-sagas-case-study left open.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_hsa.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with all three axes, Horizon, State, and Authority, highlighted."}

*Evaluation examines the state a result rests on, the resources spent across its horizon, and the authority it exercised.*
:::

Nothing built so far answers it. Authority checks establish that each action was admitted, the durable history establishes what happened, and recovery establishes which partial effects were undone or handed off; none of them judges the task. The agent's own report is self-report, the weakest closure evidence level (@sec-vol3-intro-invariant-closure), and the tests it ran during the task were visible to it and within reach of its edits. A single run is also one draw from a stochastic system, so the same repair can pass today and fail tomorrow under an identical starting state. The question the team faces is also comparative. A new configuration, `candidate_v2`, is ready, and someone must decide whether it replaces `baseline_v1` on the tasks the repair agent will receive.

This chapter builds the evaluation pipeline that turns the repair agent's trials into that decision. It begins with what one trial must establish, an acceptance contract that states which evidence credits a task and what happens when evidence is missing. Comparable fixtures and a protected grading boundary make trials interpretable, and grading assigns each criterion to a mechanical check or a calibrated judgment. Statistical rigor then turns many graded trials into claims about a configuration, with task-level sampling, paired comparison, and metrics that match how the system will be deployed.

The second half of the chapter follows the evidence past the offline comparison. Traces and their retention policies preserve what diagnosis needs within storage and privacy limits, postmortems test explanations of a failure with controlled interventions, and staged releases govern how much live traffic a candidate may see while evidence accumulates. The chapter closes by assembling every result into one evidence-backed decision about `candidate_v2`, and the first piece of that record is the acceptance contract for a single trial.

## The Task Acceptance Contract {#sec-vol3-evaluation-contract}

Consider a declared evaluation trial of the same repair task, `pool_repair_01`, starting from fixture `pool_fixture_v1` and judged by criteria version `repair_accept_v1`. The evaluated system configuration, `candidate_v2`, names the model, prompt, tools, and harness; it names a system, not a source revision. The trial produces a new candidate artifact, `ws_r19`, whose checks must refer to those exact bytes. A recovered result for `ws_r18` remains evidence about `ws_r18` only.

A **trial**\index{Evaluation trial!definition} is one execution under the declared task, fixture, system configuration, and evaluation protocol; a second execution is another trial even if those inputs are unchanged. Repeating this one repair yields more trials of one task, not more tasks, a distinction @sec-vol3-evaluation-resampling makes quantitative. First, every trial needs an explicit acceptance rule.

### Separate evidence dimensions from a pass sequence

An evaluation contract makes the task contract's required outcomes, permitted actions, and resource limits operational, stating what is checked, on which version, by which instrument, at what observation boundary, and how unavailable evidence is treated. @Tbl-vol3-eval-contract-hierarchy separates four dimensions of evidence, parallel records rather than a sequence in which an early error voids later evidence.

| Dimension             | Evidence to inspect                                                                                                                    | Consequence for the repair                                                                                     |
|:----------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Proposal validity     | Completed proposal, parsing and schema results, represented tool and arguments                                                         | An invalid configuration rejected before dispatch can be repaired; the rejection alone need not fail the trial |
| Execution behavior    | Admitted operations and attempts, endpoint outcomes, ordering, observed partial effects, and recovery history                          | An accepted request is not necessarily a finished test; a timeout can leave an operation unresolved            |
| Task outcome          | Exact candidate artifact, required defect and regression checks, final answer, and any declared qualitative rubric                     | A targeted pass supports only its coverage; a readable report cannot replace missing required checks           |
| Constraint compliance | Authority decisions and observed effects, protected-artifact checks, consumption and liability, elapsed intervals, and residual owners | Good final code does not erase a prohibited effect or satisfy an unmet cleanup or budget condition             |

: **Dimensions of Task Evaluation**: Each dimension contributes scoped evidence. The task's declared criteria determine which findings reject a trial, which remain pending, and which serve only as diagnostics. {#tbl-vol3-eval-contract-hierarchy}

A proposal with the wrong argument type can be rejected locally, corrected, and followed by a successful repair, and a task that permits such recovery still accepts the trial. A policy that forbids even proposing a particular disclosure makes that attempt a failing criterion instead. The record therefore states whether each event was a proposal, an admitted request, or an observed effect. The separation also keeps diagnostic value after acceptance is lost: when a protected-file condition fails, the test results, elapsed time, and cleanup still explain the failure, although they cannot override it.

::: {#dfn-vol3-accepted-task .callout-definition title="Accepted task"}

***Accepted task***\index{Accepted task!definition} is a task completion credited to a particular trial because the available evidence satisfies its declared outcome, process, resource, and residual-duty criteria at the required evidence level.

1. **Significance**: Acceptance is the denominator of cost per accepted task, $C_{\text{eff}}$ in @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task. Every rejected or unresolved trial's spend is charged to the accepted ones, so a looser acceptance rule lowers the reported cost without making the system cheaper.
2. **Distinction**: Passing one verifier is narrower than acceptance when other required checks, constraints, or duties remain. The task identity is distinct from the trial that attempts it.
3. **Common pitfall**: Crediting a trial from a model's completion claim, a transport status, or a test result for a different candidate revision.

:::

### State what each instrument establishes

Three sources of evidence have different limits. Runtime guards and external checks are the two halves of invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}). Runtime guards enforce bounds at the boundaries they mediate, such as withholding an unauthorized dispatch. External checks assess specified properties, such as whether the submitted candidate passes a defect reproducer and the required regression suite. Human or model judgments assess a declared rubric, such as whether the final report accurately explains its evidence, and a required rubric needs the calibration developed in @sec-vol3-evaluation-grading.

All three obey the **coverage rule**\index{Coverage rule!definition}, which states that a check establishes exactly the properties its coverage and assumptions support (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-continuations). Protecting a grader from agent modification secures the integrity of its measurement, not its coverage; a test suite can still miss a defect.

::: {#dfn-state-delta-verification .callout-definition title="State-delta verification"}

***State-delta verification***\index{State-delta verification!definition} checks specified properties of an observed change between declared initial and resulting environment states, using measurements tied to the relevant versions and task criteria.

1. **Significance**: It can distinguish a claimed repair from an observed artifact or service change that meets the selected checks.
2. **Distinction**: The change is a defined comparison, not literal subtraction of arbitrary filesystem trees or databases and not proof of every aspect of correctness.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating any nonempty patch or successful tool response as evidence that the intended change occurred without an unwanted one.

:::

The criterion selects the observation and the instrument. A read-only analysis succeeds with a supported answer and no persistent state change, while a repair can require history as well as final files, since an unauthorized deletion followed by restoration still violates a policy that forbids the deletion. Resource evidence needs named boundaries too. Execution and finalization are measured against their separate allowances from @sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting, tokens, money, and occupied resources stay separate quantities, and settled charges stay separate from outstanding reserved liability, which an evaluation cutoff neither refunds nor stops.

### Preserve mixed and incomplete verdicts

For each required criterion, retain its result and supporting evidence. Use `pass` when that evidence meets the criterion, `fail` when it establishes a violation, `pending` while a required assessment is still expected within the observation window, and `unknown` when the necessary evidence is insufficient or unavailable at the cutoff, recording why. These are evaluation verdicts, not trajectory lifecycle states.

An established failure of any mandatory criterion makes the overall verdict `fail` even if others remain unresolved. If all required criteria pass, the trial is accepted; otherwise it remains pending or unknown. This is the **four-verdict rule**\index{Four-verdict rule!definition}, and its corollary governs every count in the chapter: incomplete cases stay in the denominator under a declared rule, because dropping them changes the population being measured.

::: {#exmp-13-repair-acceptance-record .callout-example title="A targeted pass is not a completed evaluation"}

**Problem**: The trial submits `ws_r19` under `repair_accept_v1`. The contract requires the defect reproducer and designated regression checks to pass, the report to state the supported scope, permitted actions and resource allowances to hold, and temporary resources to be released or transferred under its residual-duty policy. At an interim observation, can this trial be accepted?

| Required evidence               | Observation for this trial                                                                                                                  | Verdict at this observation                                        |
|:--------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Candidate-specific defect check | The designated reproducer passed on `ws_r19`                                                                                                | `pass` for this check only                                         |
| Required regression coverage    | The designated suite has not yet produced a complete result                                                                                 | `pending`                                                          |
| Report scope                    | The declared review found that the report identifies the candidate, completed check, and missing coverage                                   | `pass` under that rubric and review                                |
| Permitted process               | Retained mediation and protected-artifact checks satisfy the specified process criteria; a malformed proposal was corrected before dispatch | `pass` within the stated coverage                                  |
| Resource criteria               | Admissions remained within the configured bounds, but required final usage evidence for an outstanding operation is not yet available       | Admission-bound check `pass`; final-accounting criterion `pending` |
| Residual duties                 | The designated service acknowledged ownership of the remaining operation and charge reconciliation, as this contract permits                | Handoff criterion `pass`; the external outcome remains unresolved  |

: **An Interim Repair Evaluation Record**: Hypothetical findings for one identified trial. Each result retains its criterion and scope; successful handoff does not establish the result of the transferred operation. {#tbl-vol3-repair-acceptance-record}

**Result**: The trial in @tbl-vol3-repair-acceptance-record is not yet accepted. Its overall verdict is `pending` because required regression and accounting evidence is still expected. If the regression suite reports a required check failure, the overall verdict becomes `fail`, while the unresolved charge remains recorded. If the observation window closes first, the affected criteria become `unknown`, a gap that neither the targeted pass nor the accepted handoff fills.

**Systems insight**: The record distinguishes task completion, runtime enforcement, grader coverage, and owned residual work, and a favorable result in one category cannot substitute for missing evidence in another.

:::

The acceptance contract states what a trial must establish. Its usefulness in a comparison still depends on the conditions under which the evidence was obtained, since a different starting repository, changed dependency, or exposed grading solution can change the score without improving the agent system.

## Hermetic Evaluation Gyms {#sec-vol3-evaluation-gyms}

To compare `candidate_v2` with `baseline_v1`, the evaluator needs more than two final reports. Both systems must meet the declared task under comparable starting conditions, and each result must be checked against the artifact its own trial produced. If one run inherits a repaired file, a changed dependency, or a still-running test from another, the observed difference no longer isolates the intended system change.

An **evaluation gym**\index{Evaluation gym!definition} provides the task's interactive environment, controlled starting conditions, and interfaces for collecting evaluation evidence. Its **hermetic boundary**\index{Hermetic boundary!definition} specifies which dependencies are supplied or controlled and which external interactions are excluded. The boundary is an experimental contract that fixes the declared conditions; a stochastic environment qualifies once its variation is declared, and neither identical model responses nor complete production fidelity is part of the promise.

### Specify the fixture before running the trial

A **task fixture**\index{Task fixture!definition} packages the initial state and dependencies needed to instantiate an evaluation task; for the repair, `pool_fixture_v1` identifies the starting repository, dependency versions, test-service behavior, and permitted task data. The fixture sets the conditions of the attempt, and the separate acceptance criteria judge its result.

@Tbl-vol3-evaluation-fixture-contract records the conditions that must accompany the trial.

| Fixture component       | What the repair evaluation declares                                                                                            | Why the comparison needs it                                          |
|:------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Initial task state      | Starting source revision, supplied defect description, permitted files and any initial service state                           | Neither system inherits another trial's fix or an undeclared hint    |
| Executable dependencies | Toolchain, packages, tool interfaces, service fixtures, and relevant configuration versions                                    | A dependency change is not mistaken for a system improvement         |
| Interaction policy      | Available tools, permitted data and destinations, resource limits, and external behaviors represented                          | Both systems face the declared task and authority boundary           |
| Variation policy        | Fixed or sampled fault conditions, scheduling and random inputs where controlled, and recorded provenance where not controlled | The experiment distinguishes intended variation from missing control |
| Evidence boundary       | Exported candidate identity, protected grader configuration, criteria version, and allowed development feedback                | A result applies to the actual submitted artifact and check          |
| Trial lifecycle         | Reset readiness, output capture, observation cutoff, cleanup and residual ownership                                            | Late work and retained state cannot silently enter the next trial    |

: **A fixture contract for comparable trials**: The manifest defines what is held fixed, what may vary, and what evidence is retained. It does not assert that every production condition is represented. {#tbl-vol3-evaluation-fixture-contract}

The comparison also declares how tasks are selected, since repeated trials of one fixture characterize only that repair (@sec-vol3-evaluation-rigor). A fixed model seed leaves serving internals and observation order free, so the record states the available provenance and the remaining variability.

### Control interactions without hiding the behavior being tested

Interactive evaluation measures the loop in which the system inspects the repository, receives diagnostics, revises a candidate, and requests checks; a static answer test leaves those interactions unexercised. The fixture follows the task, so a document-analysis fixture pins files and a retrieval collection, and a browser-task fixture adds account permissions and application state.

Real tools in an isolated fixture can exercise compilation, filesystem changes, and test execution. Stateful service emulators represent operations whose later responses depend on earlier actions. Recorded responses support a narrower replay boundary, valid only while the request, arguments, versions, and ordering match; a changed request cannot simply receive the next historical response (@sec-vol3-persistence-replay). Under this **matching-request rule**\index{Matching-request rule!definition}, the evaluator must supply behavior valid for a changed path or report the fixture's unsupported interaction.

For the repair's temporary environment, a service fixture that always returns immediate provisioning success cannot test recovery from a lost reply or delayed creation. A fault fixture instead controls whether the request reached the endpoint, when its effect occurred, and which acknowledgment was withheld, which makes the uncertainty from @sec-vol3-sagas-case-study observable. Deterministic mocks improve control but can omit contention, timing, partial effects, or unusual errors, while realistic services add setup cost and variability. Choose fidelity around the claim, and report omitted behaviors with the score, since a high score on a simplified fixture is evidence only for the conditions it represents. Evaluation against real external services needs its own authorized scope; labeling a run a benchmark grants no authority.

### Reset the state relevant to the experiment

The reset contract in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling-reset supplies the execution boundary, and evaluation adds that each admitted trial begins in conditions compatible with its fixture. Stop or account for owned writers, capture the candidate consistently, retire the old trial's authority, and reset every mutable resource the next trial could inherit; a clean repository still leaves background jobs, host-side queues, and stateful mocks. An unresolved previous operation keeps its identity and owner, and a resource that delayed work can still affect stays out of the pool, because discarding the old workspace leaves that operation unsettled.

Copy-on-write snapshots reduce repeated initialization, and reported evaluation throughput separates preparation, reset, grading, queueing, and execution, since a fast lease allocation can understate the time until a trial can begin. Declared sharing is compatible with a valid experiment. Immutable dependencies can be shared, and a warmed cache is an intentional condition when measuring warm operation. Where contention or trial order influences the endpoint, state those conditions or randomize assignment so that an uncontrolled difference is never attributed to the candidate.

### Protect the grader from the submitted code

Visible development tests give the system useful feedback. Held-out acceptance tests, the sealed tests among the closure evidence levels of @sec-vol3-intro-invariant-closure, assess the submitted artifact without exposing their complete specification as another optimization target. Keep reference solutions, protected test definitions, grading configuration, and the authoritative result store outside the agent's task environment, and bind the grading result to the exact bytes of `ws_r19` captured at a consistent boundary.

Submitted code stays untrusted after the agent process stops. If a clean grader imports the candidate package into the same interpreter as its assertions, that code can alter shared objects or the test runner. If hidden tests are mounted where candidate code can read them during execution, their confidentiality is gone, wherever they sat during the agent's run. Read-only files prevent direct edits and nothing more.

The grader design must therefore specify two boundaries, the live agent's access and the submitted artifact's execution reach. A trusted controller selects tests and collects measurements through a constrained interface while candidate code executes in a separately limited environment. The controller protects its decision logic and result storage, restricts candidate-supplied configuration and hooks under the task's patch-admission policy, which names the protected files and permitted edits, and treats candidate-produced logs as untrusted observations. @Fig-vol3-eval-gym-architecture places the trial's sandbox and this grading boundary side by side.

::: {#fig-vol3-eval-gym-architecture fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Trial Sandbox and Grading Boundary**: The agent under test edits and runs checks inside a single-use fixture whose base image is shared read-only and whose writes land in a per-trial copy-on-write layer; external egress is blocked, and service fixtures stand in for the dependencies the task declares. The captured candidate `ws_r19` crosses to a grading boundary, where a trusted controller keeps the held-out tests, criteria, and result store and sends selected tests to a separately limited execution of the candidate code. That execution remains the attack surface, because submitted code runs with the tests it receives, so its outputs are untrusted observations until the controller binds each criterion's verdict to the exact artifact." fig-alt="Two regions. Left, a task sandbox with an agent-under-test box labeled with configuration candidate_v2, an arrow labeled edits and runs checks into a fixture box holding a read-only shared base image and a copy-on-write layer for the trial's writes, and an interaction boundary box with external egress blocked and service fixtures. An arrow carries the captured artifact ws_r19, exact bytes, to the right region, a grading boundary. There a trusted controller holding held-out tests, criteria repair_accept_v1, decision logic, and the result store sends selected tests down to a dashed candidate execution box marked attack surface, which returns untrusted outputs and logs. The controller also feeds a criterion-level verdicts box listing pass, fail, pending, and unknown, bound to ws_r19."}
![](images/svg/ch13-eval-gym-architecture.svg)
:::

Some repository tests require in-process execution with the submitted code, and such a harness states that attack surface. Adversarial fixture checks probe known ways to read protected material, change the runner, or forge reported outcomes, and under the coverage rule passing them supports only the boundary they cover.

### Keep development feedback separate from evaluation evidence

Leakage can enter before or during a trial. Training data may overlap a public benchmark, a retrieval index may expose a reference solution, and prior trial memory may carry a held-out answer into the next run. Repeatedly tuning prompts against held-out failures also turns that set from independent assessment into development data,[^fn-goodhart-holdout-evaluation] because analyses chosen after seeing earlier held-out results can overfit the held-out set itself [@dwork2015reusable]. Track the provenance and allowed use of task descriptions, solutions, tests, and derived traces, including retrieval sources and retained memories. Similarity tools flag overlap for investigation, but falling below their threshold does not prove two tasks independent; @sec-vol3-trajectory-curation develops the corresponding training-split discipline.

[^fn-goodhart-holdout-evaluation]: **Goodhart's Law**: The monetary economist Charles Goodhart observed in 1975 that any observed statistical regularity tends to collapse once pressure is placed on it for control purposes [@goodhart1984]. A held-out suite used to choose among prompts has become such a control target, so its score drifts from measuring the task population toward measuring fit to the suite. The simplest remedy is procedural: retire a suite into development use once it has steered decisions, and hold a fresh one for the release claim. \index{Goodhart's law!held-out evaluation}

Three benchmarks show how fixtures and criteria fit together. SWE-bench presents repository issues and evaluates generated patches against task-specific tests [@jimenez2024swebench]. Its evaluation procedure checks both tests expected to change from failing to passing and tests expected to remain passing [@jimenez2024swebench], which grounds “repair” in behavior on a specified repository state, limited by the coverage of those tests. GAIA poses questions with one short, unambiguous answer and grades the normalized final answer by exact match [@mialon2023gaia], so the checker is cheap and exact for that property but observes nothing about the actions taken to reach it. WebArena hosts self-contained web applications and grades many tasks by querying the resulting application state rather than the agent's transcript [@zhou2024webarena]. A state assertion checks only the records it queries, so an unrelated order deleted on the way to a correct result passes unless the acceptance contract also checks for unintended mutations, which is why the constraint-compliance dimension in @tbl-vol3-eval-contract-hierarchy needs its own evidence.

::: {.callout-checkpoint title="Comparable trials and protected evidence"}

- [ ] **Identity**: Why must a result for `ws_r18` not become the grade for newly submitted `ws_r19`, even on the same task fixture?
- [ ] **Fidelity**: Which recovery claim cannot be tested by a provisioning mock that always returns immediate success?
- [ ] **Grader boundary**: Hidden tests are absent during the agent's run but share an interpreter with candidate code during grading. Which attack surface remains, and which change to the grader design closes it?
- [ ] **Reset**: A previous trial left an unresolved remote job. Would you return its sandbox to the pool, and what must be established first?
- [ ] **Leakage**: Why can repeated tuning on held-out errors weaken the evaluation even when every sandbox resets correctly?

:::

The fixture now supplies comparable interactions and a protected boundary for collecting evidence. Grading decides which checks establish each criterion and where a fallible judgment is required.

## Grading Trajectories {#sec-vol3-evaluation-grading}

Two trials of `pool_repair_01` can submit byte-identical source files and still differ in acceptance status. For `ws_r19`, only the targeted check has passed, while another trial of the same patch may already have established the regression and accounting evidence that `ws_r19` still awaits. Comparing the patches alone cannot tell the two apart. Grading connects each declared criterion to evidence, records what that evidence establishes, and preserves what remains unknown.

### Outcome and process criteria

An outcome criterion concerns the requested result, such as the regression checks against `ws_r19`; it may still inspect history when history determines the result, because a final resource count cannot establish that no duplicate allocation occurred. Process criteria concern how the trial reached its result, and the evidence that process deserves separate grading comes from reasoning tasks. On math word problems, Uesato et al. [-@uesato2022solving] found that outcome and process supervision reached similar final-answer accuracy while process supervision sharply reduced correct answers reached through flawed reasoning, and Lightman et al. [-@lightman2023let] found that process-supervised reward models selected correct solutions more reliably; @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-verification develops those verifiers. For an agent, the process also includes actions. Current authority, forbidden disclosures, required approvals, and recovery obligations can be mandatory conditions of acceptance, while other process measurements only diagnose. Tool-call validity, for example, measures the fraction of proposed calls that satisfy their schemas and is silent on whether the chosen calls were useful.

Diagnostic metrics need their own denominators and endpoints. A recovery rate counts episodes that met a stated recovery condition among the eligible episodes observed, reporting unresolved episodes separately; a different next action alone is not a recovery. Partial-credit scores show which checked subgoals were met and leave a failed mandatory condition failed, and turns, tokens, and costs are reported with the task outcomes so that a shorter failed trial never reads as an efficiency gain.

### Measure grader errors against an independent assessment

A check can reject satisfactory work or accept unsatisfactory work. The verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) separates checking a stated property from establishing that the property captures the task, so a grader's error rates must be measured rather than assumed from its repeatability. False acceptance is especially consequential when accepted trajectories support release or later training, but the two error directions answer different questions. Let $F$ denote failure of the specified criterion under an independent reference assessment, and let $\mathrm{Acc}$ denote acceptance by the grader under study. Then distinguish

$$\text{False-acceptance rate}=P(\mathrm{Acc}\mid F), \qquad
\text{Failure among accepted}=P(F\mid \mathrm{Acc}).$$

The **false-acceptance rate**\index{False acceptance rate!evaluation checks} conditions on reference-assessed failures and measures how often the grader accepted them. Failure among accepted conditions on grader acceptances and measures how often independent assessment found failure among them. A random audit of accepted outputs estimates the second quantity; the first requires reference-assessed failures, including those the grader rejected. Both need stated sampling, enough assessed cases, and an uncertainty estimate.

The distinction matters when the system changes, because failure among accepted cases depends on the prevalence and kinds of failures as well as on the grader's errors. A candidate can expose gaps that were rare in the calibration set, so each candidate's audit rechecks them rather than borrowing a historical false-acceptance rate.

Calibration cases come from the intended task population, with deliberate coverage of important failure modes, assessed independently against the same versioned rubric. Reference assessors also err, so the set keeps its adjudication procedure and unresolved labels. A set that oversamples failures reports that design, since its unweighted error fraction describes the calibration mix rather than deployment, and cases used to tune the grader stay out of it.

### Calibrate qualitative judgment

A report's adequacy or a repair explanation's clarity may require judgment rather than an exact test. A **large language model (LLM) judge**\index{LLM judge!definition} is a model used to score such criteria under a rubric, and the evaluation contract states whether its verdict is a required criterion, a signal for human review, or a diagnostic score. A favorable judgment cannot override another criterion's failure or turn unavailable evidence into a pass.

Ground the judge in trusted result records and discrete rubric items. For the repair explanation, those items can distinguish describing the patch accurately, identifying which checks ran, and acknowledging unresolved work. Candidate text and artifacts remain untrusted inputs to the grader, not instructions that may revise its rubric, and a tool-assisted judge inherits the same authority boundaries as any other tool user.

Zheng et al. [-@zheng2023judging] measured position and verbosity biases in model judges and found the evidence for self-enhancement bias inconclusive, so each judge is tested on its own workload. Pairwise judging declares order swapping, ties, and abstentions before scoring and keeps them in the denominator, and a judge from a different model family is not independent by that fact alone.

For categorical ratings of the same cases, Cohen's kappa [@cohen1960] summarizes agreement relative to the raters' marginal label frequencies:

$$\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}$$

Here $p_o$ is the observed agreement fraction, and $p_e=\sum_y p_{y,1}p_{y,2}$ uses each rater's fraction of labels in category $y$. When $p_e=1$, the expression is undefined. High raw agreement can arise from heavily concentrated label frequencies.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-evaluation-kappa-chance
#| echo: false
# CHANCE AGREEMENT UNDER A CONCENTRATED BASE RATE (LEGO)
# Goal: Show raw agreement produced with zero agreement beyond chance.
# Scope: Two raters labeling "pass" independently of the case, same marginal rate.
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_percent, check

class KappaChance:
    # 1. LOAD: hypothetical marginal pass rate shared by both raters.
    pass_rate = 0.90
    chk_rate = 0.80  # checkpoint exercise: a second hypothetical marginal rate

    # 2. EXECUTE: independence makes observed agreement equal chance agreement.
    p_o = pass_rate**2 + (1 - pass_rate) ** 2
    p_e = pass_rate * pass_rate + (1 - pass_rate) * (1 - pass_rate)
    kappa = (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e)

    # 3. GUARD: textbook arithmetic.
    check(abs(p_o - 0.82) < 1e-12, "Raw agreement from chance alone")
    check(abs(kappa) < 1e-12, "No agreement beyond chance")
    check(0.5 < chk_rate < pass_rate, "Checkpoint rate differs from the worked rate")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    pass_rate_str = fmt_percent(pass_rate, precision=0, style="prose")
    chk_rate_str = fmt_percent(chk_rate, precision=0, style="prose")
    p_o_str = fmt_percent(p_o, precision=0, style="prose")
    kappa_str = fmt(kappa, precision=0)
```

If two raters each label `{python} KappaChance.pass_rate_str` of cases as passing, independently of what the case contains, they agree on `{python} KappaChance.p_o_str` of cases by chance alone and $\kappa$ is `{python} KappaChance.kappa_str`. Report those frequencies, disagreements, and assessment coverage with kappa; the coefficient measures agreement, not whether either rater is correct.

Because shared mistakes survive high agreement, a grader's operating policy is set by the errors that matter for its role, and it is recalibrated whenever the rubric, judge, evidence interface, or evaluated population changes.

::: {.callout-checkpoint title="Defend a grading verdict"}

- [ ] **Evidence scope**: The trial's targeted check passes on `ws_r19`, but required regression and accounting evidence remain pending under `repair_accept_v1`. Which criteria are supported, and why does an acknowledged residual-duty handoff not fill those gaps?
- [ ] **Conditional denominator**: An audit samples only grader-accepted reports. Does its failure fraction estimate $P(\mathrm{Acc}\mid F)$ or $P(F\mid \mathrm{Acc})$? What population is missing for the other estimate?
- [ ] **Process requirement**: When can a recovered malformed proposal remain a diagnostic event, and when must a process violation reject the trial despite a correct final artifact?
- [ ] **Agreement vs. truth**: Two judges each pass `{python} KappaChance.chk_rate_str` of reports, independently of what the reports contain. Estimate their raw agreement and $\kappa$, and decide whether that agreement supports using either one as an acceptance grader.

:::

Grading yields criterion-level verdicts and diagnostic measurements for the observed trials. Generalizing beyond those trials is a statistical question.

## Statistical Evaluation Rigor {#sec-vol3-evaluation-rigor}

Suppose `candidate_v2` accepts a few more sampled tasks than `baseline_v1` in one sweep. That gain can be noise, while a smaller gain can be informative when the comparison preserves which tasks changed outcome. Deciding which requires naming the population the result should describe and accounting for variation in both the tasks and their executions, so the uncertainty that matters belongs to the comparison rather than to each system's separate score.

### Distinguish tasks from repeated runs {#sec-vol3-evaluation-resampling}

A task identifies a problem and its declared fixture and criteria; a run is one execution of a system configuration on that task. Another artifact for the connection-pool repair is another run of the same task. Model sampling and permitted environmental variation produce different outcomes on repeated runs, even at a fixed seed or temperature (@sec-vol3-persistence-replay).

Let $p_i$ be a fixed system's probability of acceptance on task $i$ under the declared execution and grading protocol. Suppose tasks are independently sampled from a specified population, and $R$ runs are independent conditional on each task. For the mean across $N$ tasks with the same number of runs per task,

$$\operatorname{Var}(\hat p)=\frac{\sigma^2_{\mathrm{task}}}{N}+\frac{\sigma^2_{\mathrm{run}}}{NR},\qquad
\sigma^2_{\mathrm{task}}=\operatorname{Var}(p_i),\quad
\sigma^2_{\mathrm{run}}=\mathbb E[p_i(1-p_i)].$$ {#eq-variance-decomposition}

The first term in @eq-variance-decomposition reflects task difficulty; the second reflects execution variation within a task. More repeats shrink only the second term, while more independently sampled tasks shrink both. Once $R$ exceeds $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{run}}/\sigma^2_{\mathrm{task}}$, the run term is already the smaller one, and the next unit of evaluation budget buys more precision as new tasks than as repeats.

A fixed benchmark suite supports a narrower target, mean performance on those particular tasks, which repeated runs can estimate more precisely without making the suite representative of future work. Related tasks from one repository, shared service outages, or cross-trial state leakage also violate independent-task assumptions, so the analysis preserves those clusters rather than counting every run as a new task.

### Estimate one acceptance probability {#sec-vol3-evaluation-wilson}

For one run on each independently sampled task, let $X$ of $N$ trials be accepted, so $\hat p=X/N$ estimates the population acceptance probability. A confidence interval expresses uncertainty from this sampling model only; grader error, missing outcomes, contamination, and a changed task distribution need their own accounting.

The familiar Wald interval, $\hat p\pm z\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/N}$, breaks down at the extreme rates that safety and reliability claims involve. When every observed outcome agrees, as in a clean safety record, it collapses to zero width, and near the boundaries it can extend below zero.[^fn-wald-interval-coverage] The **Wilson score interval**\index{Wilson score interval!definition} [@wilson1927probable] avoids both failures by using the hypothesized rate, not the observed one, in the variance:[^fn-wilson-score-inversion]

$$\tilde p=\frac{X+z^2/2}{N+z^2},\qquad
[L,U]=\tilde p\pm\frac{z}{N+z^2}\sqrt{\frac{X(N-X)}{N}+\frac{z^2}{4}}.$$ {#eq-wilson-interval}

Here $z$ is the standard normal quantile for the selected two-sided confidence level.

[^fn-wilson-score-inversion]: **Wilson score inversion**\index{Wilson score interval!test inversion}: With $z=z_{1-\alpha/2}$, the score interval contains the values $p\in[0,1]$ satisfying $N(\hat p-p)^2\le z^2p(1-p)$. Solving this quadratic inequality gives the endpoints: the variance uses the hypothesized $p$, rather than fixing it at $\hat p$ as in the Wald construction [@guthrie2020nisthandbook, sec. 7.2.4.1].

[^fn-wald-interval-coverage]: **Wald Interval Coverage**: A systematic study of binomial intervals found that the Wald interval's actual coverage oscillates erratically with both $N$ and $p$, stays poor at sample sizes that textbook rules of thumb call safe, and recommended the Wilson interval for small samples [@brown2001interval]. Agent evaluation lives in exactly that regime: suites of tens of tasks, and violation rates near zero, where a nominal 95 percent Wald interval can promise far more than it delivers. \index{Wald interval!coverage failure}

For zero acceptances in 50 independent tasks, @eq-wilson-interval gives a lower limit of zero and an upper limit of $z^2/(50+z^2)$, which panel B of @fig-vol3-sample-size-confidence-intervals marks. Read with the outcomes reversed, the same arithmetic prices a clean record: zero observed violations in 50 tasks remains consistent with a violation rate up to that limit.

The binary examples here assume complete verdicts. A study with pending or unknown verdicts declares its cutoff and missing-outcome analysis before counting, since dropping them biases the sample toward tasks that finish or grade easily.

### Compare paired outcomes {#sec-vol3-evaluation-paired}

Run the baseline and candidate on separate, comparably initialized executions of each sampled task, with matched criteria and allowances, and keep each task's pair of outcomes together. @Tbl-vol3-mcnemar-contingency organizes a hypothetical complete comparison drawn from a prespecified cohort that never included the pending `ws_r19` trial.

| Baseline outcome | Candidate accepted | Candidate rejected |
|:-----------------|:-------------------|:-------------------|
| Accepted         | $n_{11}=70$        | $b=12$             |
| Rejected         | $c=18$             | $n_{00}=50$        |

: **Paired task outcomes**: One baseline run and one candidate run on each of 150 independently sampled tasks. Counts are illustrative, with no missing verdicts; execution order and fixtures follow the prespecified comparison protocol. {#tbl-vol3-mcnemar-contingency}

The baseline's accepted count is $n_{11}+b$ and the candidate's is $n_{11}+c$. The observed difference is

$$\hat\Delta=\hat p_{\mathrm{cand}}-\hat p_{\mathrm{base}}=\frac{c-b}{N}.$$

The discordant pairs determine the net gain, while the concordant pairs still count in $N$ and in the uncertainty. The marginal counts alone cannot reveal whether the candidate gained tasks without losing any or traded many wins for many losses.

**McNemar's test**\index{McNemar's test!definition}[^fn-mcnemar-paired-test] [@mcnemar1947note] asks whether the paired marginal probabilities are equal. Under that null, and conditional on $n_{\mathrm{disc}}=b+c>0$ discordant pairs, candidate wins are $\operatorname{Binomial}(n_{\mathrm{disc}},1/2)$, and the exact two-sided test sums the symmetric tails:

$$p_{\mathrm{exact}}=\min\!\left(1,\;2\sum_{j=0}^{\min(b,c)}\binom{n_{\mathrm{disc}}}{j}2^{-n_{\mathrm{disc}}}\right).$$

[^fn-mcnemar-paired-test]: **McNemar's Test**: The test was introduced for psychological measurements in which the same subjects are classified twice, so the two proportions are correlated and cannot be compared as independent samples. Its central move is to discard concordant pairs from the test statistic, since a task both configurations pass, or both fail, says nothing about which is better. The interval for $\Delta$ still uses those pairs, because they set the precision of the estimate. \index{McNemar's test!concordant pairs}

A release decision usually asks a magnitude question instead of an equality question. **Noninferiority**\index{Noninferiority!definition} is the claim that the candidate loses no more than a declared tolerance $\delta_{\mathrm{tol}}$, and it needs an interval $[L_\Delta,U_\Delta]$ for $\Delta$ itself. The worksheet uses Newcombe's paired-score method 10 [@newcombe1998improved], which combines the candidate and baseline Wilson intervals of @eq-wilson-interval through a continuity-corrected estimate of their within-pair correlation, so that shared task outcomes narrow the interval even when both marginal counts stay fixed. The result is nominal and approximate, valid for one prespecified look under independent paired sampling. @Sec-vol3-appendix-math-newcombe states the interval in full, and the paired bootstrap [@efron1979bootstrap] of @sec-vol3-appendix-math-bootstrap serves statistics that lack such an analytic interval.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-evaluation-paired-comparison
#| echo: false
# PAIRED ACCEPTANCE DIFFERENCE (LEGO)
# Goal: Estimate one rate and compare paired configurations at a fixed endpoint.
# Scope: Illustrative independent task pairs, complete verdicts, fixed protocol.
from math import sqrt, comb, ceil
from statistics import NormalDist
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_percent, check

def evaluation_wilson(x, n, z):
    if not isinstance(x, int) or not isinstance(n, int) or not 0 <= x <= n or n <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Require integer counts 0 <= x <= n and n > 0")
    center = (x + z * z / 2) / (n + z * z)
    spread = z * sqrt(x * (n - x) / n + z * z / 4) / (n + z * z)
    return max(0.0, center - spread), min(1.0, center + spread)

def evaluation_paired_score(n11, b, c, n00, z):
    # Newcombe (1998), method 10. b=baseline-only; c=candidate-only.
    cells = (n11, b, c, n00)
    if any(not isinstance(v, int) or v < 0 for v in cells) or sum(cells) <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Require nonnegative integer cells and positive total")
    n = sum(cells)
    pc, pb = (n11 + c) / n, (n11 + b) / n
    lc, uc = evaluation_wilson(n11 + c, n, z)
    lb, ub = evaluation_wilson(n11 + b, n, z)
    denominator = sqrt((n11 + c) * (b + n00) * (n11 + b) * (c + n00))
    numerator = n11 * n00 - b * c
    if numerator > 0:
        numerator = max(numerator - n / 2, 0)
    rho = numerator / denominator if denominator else 0.0
    lower_width = sqrt(max(0.0, (pc - lc) ** 2 + (ub - pb) ** 2 - 2 * rho * (pc - lc) * (ub - pb)))
    upper_width = sqrt(max(0.0, (uc - pc) ** 2 + (pb - lb) ** 2 - 2 * rho * (uc - pc) * (pb - lb)))
    return pc - pb, pc - pb - lower_width, pc - pb + upper_width

class PairedAcceptance:
    # 1. LOAD: prespecified illustrative counts, nominal level, and tolerance.
    n11, b, c, n00 = 70, 12, 18, 50
    z = NormalDist().inv_cdf(0.975)
    tolerance = 0.02  # acceptable loss chosen before seeing outcomes

    # 2. EXECUTE: two-sided interval and exact conditional equality test.
    n = n11 + b + c + n00
    delta, lower, upper = evaluation_paired_score(n11, b, c, n00, z)
    discordant = b + c
    tail_count = 0
    for j in range(min(b, c) + 1):
        tail_count += comb(discordant, j)
    exact_p = min(1.0, 2 * tail_count / 2**discordant) if discordant else 1.0
    noninferiority = lower > -tolerance
    zero_upper = evaluation_wilson(0, 50, z)[1]
    # Planning: lower half-width scales as 1/sqrt(N); what N clears the margin?
    lower_width = delta - lower
    n_if_gain_holds = ceil(n * (lower_width / (delta + tolerance)) ** 2)
    n_if_no_gain = ceil(n * (lower_width / tolerance) ** 2)

    # 3. GUARD: arithmetic plus independent published method-10 examples.
    check(n == 150 and n11 + b == 82 and n11 + c == 88, "Paired totals")
    check(abs(delta - 0.04) < 1e-12, "Candidate-minus-baseline direction")
    check(abs(lower - (-0.032062854)) < 1e-8 and abs(upper - 0.111211210) < 1e-8, "Worksheet interval")
    check(not noninferiority and lower < 0 < upper, "Inconclusive gate and superiority")
    check(abs(zero_upper - z * z / (50 + z * z)) < 1e-12, "Wilson zero-count algebra")
    check(n < n_if_gain_holds < 2 * n < n_if_no_gain, "Planning counts ordered")
    for cells, expected in [((20, 2, 12, 16), (0.0562, 0.3292)), ((27, 0, 0, 27), (-0.0351, 0.0351))]:
        _, lo, hi = evaluation_paired_score(*cells, z)
        check(abs(lo - expected[0]) < 0.00005 and abs(hi - expected[1]) < 0.00005, "Newcombe Table III")

    # 4. OUTPUT: all formatted exports are consumed below.
    n_str = fmt_int(n)
    b_str, c_str = fmt_int(b), fmt_int(c)
    zero_upper_str = fmt_percent(zero_upper, precision=2, style="prose")
    delta_pp_str = fmt_int(round(100 * delta))
    lower_pp_str = fmt(100 * lower, precision=2)
    upper_pp_str = fmt(100 * upper, precision=2)
    tolerance_pp_str = fmt(100 * tolerance, precision=0)
    exact_p_str = fmt(exact_p, precision=3)
    lower_width_pp_str = fmt(100 * lower_width, precision=2)
    clear_width_pp_str = fmt(100 * (delta + tolerance), precision=0)
    n_if_gain_holds_str = fmt_int(n_if_gain_holds)
    n_if_no_gain_str = fmt_int(round(n_if_no_gain, -2))
```

::: {#nbk-vol3-evaluation-wilson-superiority .callout-notebook title="A paired gain and an inconclusive gate"}

**Problem**: For the `{python} PairedAcceptance.n_str` task pairs in @tbl-vol3-mcnemar-contingency, does the candidate establish noninferiority under a prespecified tolerance of `{python} PairedAcceptance.tolerance_pp_str` percentage points, that is, $L_\Delta>-\delta_{\mathrm{tol}}$ for the lower endpoint of a nominal 95 percent paired-score interval? If not, how many pairs would the gate need?

**Math**: The observed gain is $\hat\Delta=(c-b)/N=$ (`{python} PairedAcceptance.c_str` $-$ `{python} PairedAcceptance.b_str`)/`{python} PairedAcceptance.n_str`, or `{python} PairedAcceptance.delta_pp_str` points. Method 10 gives the interval from `{python} PairedAcceptance.lower_pp_str` to `{python} PairedAcceptance.upper_pp_str` points, so the lower half-width $\hat\Delta-L_\Delta$ is `{python} PairedAcceptance.lower_width_pp_str` points. Clearing the gate needs that half-width below $\hat\Delta+\delta_{\mathrm{tol}}$, `{python} PairedAcceptance.clear_width_pp_str` points. Half-widths shrink as $1/\sqrt N$, so the required count is $N'\approx N\left[(\hat\Delta-L_\Delta)/(\hat\Delta+\delta_{\mathrm{tol}})\right]^2$.

**Result**: The lower endpoint lies below $-\delta_{\mathrm{tol}}$, so the gate is not met, and the interval includes zero, so superiority is not established either. The exact two-sided McNemar value, `{python} PairedAcceptance.exact_p_str`, answers the separate equality question.

**Systems insight**: The candidate is held, and the knob that moves the decision is the planned number of pairs. A `{python} PairedAcceptance.delta_pp_str`-point gain that holds needs about `{python} PairedAcceptance.n_if_gain_holds_str` pairs; a true gain of zero needs the half-width inside the `{python} PairedAcceptance.tolerance_pp_str`-point tolerance itself, about `{python} PairedAcceptance.n_if_no_gain_str` pairs. Plan that count before collecting data, because rerunning the same comparison until one look passes is a different, uncalibrated test.

:::

Those planning counts follow from one scaling law. For one rate, the half-width is about $z\sqrt{p(1-p)/N}$, largest at $p=1/2$, so precision improves only as $1/\sqrt{N}$ and halving the half-width takes four times as many tasks. Detecting a difference is more demanding than estimating a rate. For two independent arms with average acceptance probability $\bar p$, target difference $\Delta$, two-sided significance $\alpha$, and power $1-\beta$, a standard planning estimate of the tasks needed per arm is

$$N_{\text{arm}}\approx\frac{2\,(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta})^2\,\bar p(1-\bar p)}{\Delta^2}.$$ {#eq-vol3-eval-planning-power}

@Sec-vol3-appendix-math-bootstrap derives the pooled form of @eq-vol3-eval-planning-power and states its assumptions.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-evaluation-sample-size-scale
#| echo: false
# HOW MANY TASKS A CLAIM NEEDS (LEGO)
# Goal: Give the magnitude of one-rate precision, two-arm detection, and pairing.
# Scope: Planning approximations at hypothetical rates; independent tasks.
from math import sqrt, ceil
from statistics import NormalDist
from mlsysim.physics.statistics import calc_two_proportion_sample_size
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, check

class SampleSizeScale:
    # 1. LOAD: worst-case rate, targets, and the worked paired table's cells.
    p_half = 0.5
    z95 = NormalDist().inv_cdf(0.975)
    small_n = 100
    target_half_width = 0.02
    alpha, power = 0.05, 0.80
    z_alpha, z_beta = 1.96, 0.84  # rounded quantiles for these targets
    delta_large, delta_small = 0.04, 0.02
    n11, b, c, n00 = 70, 12, 18, 50  # the worked paired-outcome table

    # 2. EXECUTE: one-rate half-widths, two-arm counts, paired variance.
    half_small = z95 * sqrt(p_half * (1 - p_half) / small_n)
    wilson_lo, wilson_hi = evaluation_wilson(50, small_n, z95)
    wilson_half_small = (wilson_hi - wilson_lo) / 2
    n_for_target = ceil(z95**2 * p_half * (1 - p_half) / target_half_width**2)
    arm_large = calc_two_proportion_sample_size(p_half, delta_large, z_alpha=z_alpha, z_beta=z_beta)
    arm_small = calc_two_proportion_sample_size(p_half, delta_small, z_alpha=z_alpha, z_beta=z_beta)
    arm_large_n, arm_small_n = round(arm_large), round(arm_small)
    pairs = n11 + b + c + n00
    p_cand, p_base = (n11 + c) / pairs, (n11 + b) / pairs
    discordant = (b + c) / pairs
    diff = p_cand - p_base
    var_paired = discordant - diff**2
    var_independent = p_cand * (1 - p_cand) + p_base * (1 - p_base)
    paired_share = var_paired / var_independent
    paired_half = z95 * sqrt(var_paired / pairs)
    independent_mult = var_independent / var_paired

    # 3. GUARD: scaling law, published-formula arithmetic, and pairing algebra.
    check(abs(NormalDist().inv_cdf(1 - alpha / 2) - z_alpha) < 0.005, "Rounded significance quantile")
    check(abs(NormalDist().inv_cdf(power) - z_beta) < 0.005, "Rounded power quantile")
    check(abs(half_small - 0.098) < 0.0005, "Half-width at N=100, p=0.5")
    check(abs(wilson_half_small - half_small) < 0.003, "Wilson close to normal at p=0.5")
    check(n_for_target == 2401, "Tasks for a 2-point half-width")
    check(abs(arm_large - 2450) < 1e-6 and abs(arm_small - 9800) < 1e-6, "Two-arm planning counts")
    check(abs(arm_small / arm_large - 4) < 1e-9, "Halving the difference quadruples N")
    check(abs(discordant - 0.2) < 1e-12 and abs(diff - 0.04) < 1e-12, "Worked-table discordance")
    check(0.35 < paired_share < 0.45, "Pairing removes most of the variance")
    check(abs(paired_half - 0.0713) < 0.0005, "Matches the worked interval's scale")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    small_n_str = fmt_int(small_n)
    alpha_str = fmt_percent(alpha, precision=0, style="prose")
    power_str = fmt_percent(power, precision=0, style="prose")
    half_small_pp_str = fmt(100 * half_small, precision=1)
    wilson_half_pp_str = fmt(100 * wilson_half_small, precision=1)
    target_pp_str = fmt(100 * target_half_width, precision=0)
    n_for_target_str = fmt_int(n_for_target)
    delta_large_pp_str = fmt(100 * delta_large, precision=0)
    delta_small_pp_str = fmt(100 * delta_small, precision=0)
    arm_large_str = fmt_int(arm_large_n)
    arm_small_str = fmt_int(arm_small_n)
    discordant_str = fmt_percent(discordant, precision=0, style="prose")
    paired_share_str = fmt_percent(round(paired_share, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    paired_half_pp_str = fmt(100 * paired_half, precision=1)
    independent_mult_str = fmt_multiple(independent_mult, precision=1)
```

At $p=0.5$ and 95 percent confidence, `{python} SampleSizeScale.small_n_str` independent tasks give a half-width of about `{python} SampleSizeScale.half_small_pp_str` percentage points (the Wilson interval gives `{python} SampleSizeScale.wilson_half_pp_str`), and a half-width of `{python} SampleSizeScale.target_pp_str` points needs `{python} SampleSizeScale.n_for_target_str` tasks. With a `{python} SampleSizeScale.alpha_str` two-sided significance target and `{python} SampleSizeScale.power_str` power at $\bar p=0.5$, @eq-vol3-eval-planning-power asks for about `{python} SampleSizeScale.arm_large_str` tasks per arm to detect a `{python} SampleSizeScale.delta_large_pp_str`-point difference and `{python} SampleSizeScale.arm_small_str` per arm for a `{python} SampleSizeScale.delta_small_pp_str`-point difference. @Fig-vol3-sample-size-confidence-intervals plots that $1/\sqrt{N}$ contraction and, at a small sample, shows where the Wald interval fails and the Wilson interval does not.

::: {#fig-vol3-sample-size-confidence-intervals fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**How Many Tasks an Interval Needs**: Panel A plots the normal-approximation half-width at 95 percent confidence against the number of independent tasks for three acceptance probabilities. At $p=0.5$, `{python} SampleSizeScale.small_n_str` tasks give about $\pm$`{python} SampleSizeScale.half_small_pp_str` points, and `{python} SampleSizeScale.n_for_target_str` tasks reach the dashed $\pm$`{python} SampleSizeScale.target_pp_str`-point target. Panel B compares Wald and Wilson intervals, in percent, for 50 tasks. With no acceptances, the Wald interval collapses to zero width, while the Wilson upper limit is `{python} PairedAcceptance.zero_upper_str`. With two acceptances, the Wald lower limit falls below zero, an impossible probability. At 25 acceptances the two intervals nearly coincide." fig-alt="Two panels. Panel A: line chart of normal-approximation half-width in points, from 0 to 20, against independent tasks from 0 to 2,500, with a solid curve for p equal to 0.5, a dashed curve for 0.2, and a dotted curve for 0.05. All three fall steeply and then flatten. Two points on the p equal to 0.5 curve are labeled, one at 100 tasks and one where the curve meets a dashed horizontal line at 2 points. Panel B: three rows of horizontal interval bars at 50 tasks, each comparing a gray Wald interval with a blue Wilson interval. With 0 successes, Wald is a single point at zero, labeled zero width, and Wilson extends from zero to a labeled upper limit. With 2 successes, the Wald bar extends into a shaded region below zero, labeled lower limit below 0, and the Wilson bar stays above zero. With 25 successes, the two bars nearly coincide around 50 percent."}
![](images/svg/sample_size_confidence_intervals.svg)
:::

Pairing changes the count. Each task's candidate-minus-baseline outcome takes the value $-1$, $0$, or $+1$, so with discordant fraction $\psi$ the paired estimate has variance $(\psi-\Delta^2)/N$. The worked table has `{python} SampleSizeScale.discordant_str` discordant pairs, which puts the paired variance at about `{python} SampleSizeScale.paired_share_str` of the variance two independent arms would have at the same acceptance rates. The same precision therefore needs well under half as many tasks, and the worked interval spans about $\pm$`{python} SampleSizeScale.paired_half_pp_str` points. Estimation, detection, and noninferiority thus need different counts, and a paired plan also rests on an assumed discordance rate that the study must later report as observed.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_eval_margin_paired_variance.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars. A gray bar labeled independent arms is full length and labeled 100 percent. A purple bar labeled paired tasks is well under half as long, with its percentage printed inside and the word variance beside it."}

*Pairing the worked comparison leaves about `{python} SampleSizeScale.paired_share_str` of the independent-arm variance.*
:::

The comparison so far uses one run per configuration per task. Permitting multiple attempts changes what success means and what it costs.

### Potential and repeated-run consistency {#sec-vol3-evaluation-pass-k}

A pool containing one acceptable repair, a selector returning that repair, and a system completing the same task reliably are three different outcomes. @Sec-vol3-test-time-compute-pass-at-k defined pass@$k$ as candidate availability, the probability that a pool of $k$ runs contains a passing member. Work that recurs, such as the same policy question answered in session after session, needs the opposite quantifier: every run must pass. The two belong in one statement, because they move in opposite directions as $k$ grows.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-evaluation-pass-pow-k-collapse
#| echo: false
# REPEATED-RUN CONSISTENCY ON ONE TASK (LEGO)
# Goal: Show how quickly all-k consistency falls below single-run success.
# Scope: One fixed task, independent runs under the declared reset.
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, check

class PassPowK:
    # 1. LOAD: hypothetical single-run acceptance probabilities and recurrences.
    p_hi, p_lo = 0.90, 0.80
    p_better = 0.95  # after halving the single-run failure rate
    k = 8
    target = 0.90  # consistency the recurring work must hold
    chk_p, chk_k = 0.95, 5  # checkpoint exercise givens
    # Point-in-time values reported in the tau-bench abstract (Yao et al. 2024,
    # arXiv:2406.12045): best tested agent <50% task success, pass^8 <25% (retail).
    taubench_success_bound, taubench_pow_bound, taubench_k = 0.50, 0.25, 8

    # 2. EXECUTE
    pow_hi, pow_lo, pow_better = p_hi**k, p_lo**k, p_better**k
    at_k_hi = 1 - (1 - p_hi) ** k
    p_needed = target ** (1 / k)
    fail_cut = (1 - p_hi) / (1 - p_needed)

    # 3. GUARD
    check(0.42 < pow_hi < 0.44 and 0.16 < pow_lo < 0.18, "Eight-run consistency")
    check(at_k_hi > 0.999, "Availability near one")
    check(0.986 < p_needed < 0.988 and 7 < fail_cut < 8, "Rate needed for the target")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    p_hi_str = fmt(p_hi, precision=1)
    p_hi_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_hi, precision=0, style="prose")
    p_lo_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_lo, precision=0, style="prose")
    p_better_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_better, precision=0, style="prose")
    k_str = fmt_int(k)
    target_str = fmt_percent(target, precision=0, style="prose")
    pow_hi_str = fmt_percent(round(pow_hi, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    pow_lo_str = fmt_percent(round(pow_lo, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    pow_better_str = fmt_percent(round(pow_better, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    at_k_hi_str = fmt_percent(round(at_k_hi, 4), precision=0, style="prose")
    p_needed_str = fmt_percent(p_needed, precision=1, style="prose")
    fail_needed_str = fmt_percent(1 - p_needed, precision=1, style="prose")
    fail_cut_mult_str = fmt_multiple(fail_cut, precision=1)
    chk_p_str = fmt_percent(chk_p, precision=0, style="prose")
    chk_k_str = fmt_int(chk_k)
    taubench_success_bound_str = fmt_percent(taubench_success_bound, precision=0, style="prose")
    taubench_pow_bound_str = fmt_percent(taubench_pow_bound, precision=0, style="prose")
    taubench_k_str = fmt_int(taubench_k)
```

::: {#thrm-vol3-evaluation-pass-at-k-pass-pow-k .callout-theorem title="Availability and consistency over repeated runs"}

*For a fixed task $i$, initial-state distribution, complete generation policy, and binary pass criterion, let runs be independent and identically distributed given the task, each passing with probability $p_i$.* Averaged over the declared task distribution, the probability that at least one of $k$ runs passes and the probability that all $k$ pass, **pass$^k$** or **repeated-run consistency**\index{Repeated-run consistency!definition}, are estimated from $n_i\ge k$ fully graded runs with $c_i$ passes by the unbiased subset estimators [@chen2021evaluating; @yao2024taubench]

$$\operatorname{pass@}k=\mathbb{E}_i\left[1-(1-p_i)^k\right],\qquad
\widehat q_{i,k}=1-\frac{\binom{n_i-c_i}{k}}{\binom{n_i}{k}},$$ {#eq-pass-at-k}

$$\operatorname{pass}^{k}=\mathbb{E}_i\left[p_i^k\right],\qquad
\widehat r_{i,k}=\frac{\binom{c_i}{k}}{\binom{n_i}{k}}.$$ {#eq-pass-pow-k}

*   **Task pass probability** ($p_i$): Single-run acceptance under the declared reset and grading protocol.
*   **Claim size** ($k$): Runs the claim covers, a pool for pass@$k$ and recurrences for pass$^k$.
*   **Graded runs** ($n_i$, $c_i$): Runs generated for the estimate and the number that passed; each binomial numerator is zero when $n_i-c_i<k$ or $c_i<k$, respectively.

Because pass@$k$ rises with $k$ while pass$^k$ falls, the same system can look near perfect or unreliable depending on which quantifier the claim needs, as notebook \ref{nbk-vol3-evaluation-pass-pow-k} shows numerically.

:::

Each subset in @eq-pass-at-k contributes one when it contains a pass, and each in @eq-pass-pow-k when all its members pass, so their expectations are $1-(1-p_i)^k$ and $p_i^k$; @sec-vol3-appendix-math-pass-at-k derives both by indicator averaging and gives product forms that avoid factorial overflow. Average task-level estimates with the declared task weights, never by repeat count. The pass@$k$ metric measures candidate availability, while the deployed selector's returned results are measured separately (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-pass-at-k); pass$^k$ can describe complete system runs, selector included. The consistency metric entered agent benchmarking with $\tau$-bench, which reports it for tool-using agents in customer-service domains[^fn-taubench-consistency-gap] [@yao2024taubench].

[^fn-taubench-consistency-gap]: **Consistency on a Live Benchmark**: At the benchmark's 2024 introduction, its authors reported that the strongest function-calling agent they tested completed fewer than `{python} PassPowK.taubench_success_bound_str` of tasks, and that its pass$^k$ at $k$ equal to `{python} PassPowK.taubench_k_str` fell below `{python} PassPowK.taubench_pow_bound_str` in the retail domain [@yao2024taubench]. The specific agents will age; the pattern will not, because consistency over repeated sessions always sits below single-run success once any task passes with probability below one. \index{Repeated-run consistency!benchmark evidence}

::: {#nbk-vol3-evaluation-pass-pow-k .callout-notebook title="Single-run success is not reliability"}

**Problem**: A system accepts a recurring task on `{python} PassPowK.p_hi_pct_str` of single runs. How often does it pass all `{python} PassPowK.k_str` recurrences, and what single-run rate would hold `{python} PassPowK.target_str` consistency?

**Math**: By @eq-pass-pow-k for one task, pass$^k=p^k$. With $p$ equal to `{python} PassPowK.p_hi_str` and $k$ equal to `{python} PassPowK.k_str`, that is about `{python} PassPowK.pow_hi_str`; at `{python} PassPowK.p_lo_pct_str` it falls to about `{python} PassPowK.pow_lo_str`. Availability over the same runs, $1-(1-p)^k$, is effectively `{python} PassPowK.at_k_hi_str`. Holding `{python} PassPowK.target_str` requires $p\ge P_{\text{target}}^{1/k}$, about `{python} PassPowK.p_needed_str`.

**Systems insight**: Recurrences compound exactly as turns do in @eq-vol3-horizon-compounding, so consistency is set by the single-run failure rate raised to the number of recurrences. Halving that failure rate to reach `{python} PassPowK.p_better_pct_str` lifts pass$^k$ only to `{python} PassPowK.pow_better_str`; holding `{python} PassPowK.target_str` needs single-run failure of `{python} PassPowK.fail_needed_str`, a `{python} PassPowK.fail_cut_mult_str` cut. Recurring work therefore buys reliability most cheaply with a check that catches a failed run before delivery, which turns a failed recurrence into a retry.

:::

The distance between the two quantifiers, availability near one against consistency of `{python} PassPowK.pow_hi_str`, is the **verification gap**\index{Verification gap!definition}. A selector with a reliable checker converts availability into one accepted delivery at the cost priced in @sec-vol3-evaluation-matched-budgets; work that must pass every time it recurs gets only consistency.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_eval_margin_pass_k_diverge.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two lines from k equals 1 to k equals 8 that start at the same point near the top. The blue pass at k line rises to 100 percent; the purple pass hat k line falls steadily to a labeled dot about halfway down."}

*At `{python} PassPowK.p_hi_pct_str` per run, availability nears certainty while `{python} PassPowK.k_str`-run consistency falls to `{python} PassPowK.pow_hi_str`.*
:::

A sequence of $k$ independently drawn *new tasks* has all-success probability $(\mathbb{E}_i[p_i])^k$, which Jensen's inequality places at or below $\mathbb{E}_i[p_i^k]$, so repeating one task overstates consistency across new tasks whenever difficulty varies. Shared outages, state carried between runs, or feedback-conditioned revisions break these independence formulas, and @tbl-vol3-statistical-metrics names the experiment behind each quantity.

| Reported quantity   | Sampling unit and question                                                               | What it does not establish                          |
|:--------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| pass@$k$            | One task's pool: does at least one member pass the declared criterion?                   | That the deployed selector returns it within budget |
| Selected acceptance | One complete system trial: does the actual returned result meet the acceptance contract? | That every future run or task will pass             |
| pass$^k$            | One task repeated $k$ times: do all runs pass?                                           | Success across $k$ independently drawn new tasks    |
| Budgeted acceptance | One complete policy trial under stated resource limits                                   | The best score achievable by any policy             |

: **Metrics name different experiments**: The criterion, task distribution, reset and dependence assumptions, and treatment of unresolved verdicts accompany every score. {#tbl-vol3-statistical-metrics}

Where a verdict in the pool stays pending or unknown, report that count and the bounds obtained by assigning unresolved cases to either outcome. Which row of @tbl-vol3-statistical-metrics a claim needs depends on how the work is used, and the four lighthouse workloads (\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}, \ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}, \ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}, and \ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}) use it differently.

::: {#lhs-vol3-evaluation-evidence-by-archetype .callout-lighthouse title="Evidence standard by archetype"}

| Workload          | Checker the task admits                                              | Metric the claim needs                                                       | Binding evidence limit                                                   |
|:------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Repair agent      | Sealed regression and defect tests on the exact submitted artifact   | Selected acceptance under budget; pass@$k$ only with the checker in the loop | Test coverage, and grader isolation from submitted code                  |
| Research agent    | Rubric scored by a calibrated judge; citation checks against sources | Selected acceptance with the judge's error rates reported                    | Judge false-acceptance rate on untrusted retrieved content               |
| Remediation agent | State-delta checks on an isolated replica; approval records          | pass$^k$ over recurring incident classes, with zero forbidden effects        | Irreversible writes that no shadow fixture can exercise                  |
| Support agent     | Policy-grounded rubric per answer                                    | pass$^k$ across sessions asking the same policy question                     | Consistency over many short sessions, measured only on live-like traffic |

: **Evidence standard by workload**: Each workload's checker determines which metric its claims can support, and each carries a different limit on what its evaluation can establish. {#tbl-vol3-evaluation-evidence-by-archetype}

**Systems insight**: @Tbl-vol3-evaluation-evidence-by-archetype shows that the archetype decides the quantifier. The repair agent can buy acceptance with checked retries, so it reports selected acceptance priced through $C_{\text{eff}}$. The support agent cannot retry a wrong policy answer once a customer has read it, so its claim is pass$^k$ (notebook \ref{nbk-vol3-evaluation-pass-pow-k}). The research agent's number is only as good as its judge, and the remediation agent's release rests on hard limits that statistics cannot supply.

:::

### Comparing at matched budgets {#sec-vol3-evaluation-matched-budgets}

Fix the task distribution, criteria, and resource envelope before comparing policies. An experiment that isolates a prompt change holds the rest of the configuration fixed; one that compares complete policies lets each spend the same envelope differently among generation, checking, and repair, so equal budgets need not mean equal sample counts. Report allowances and actual use, with time and tokens separate from monetary charges, since leaderboards that rank accuracy alone reward needlessly costly agent designs [@kapoor2024agents].

For a fixed complete policy $\pi$, let $\mathrm{Acc}_\pi$ indicate accepted completion under the declared criteria, $C_\pi$ its total monetary charge, and $B$ a monetary ceiling. Its budgeted acceptance is

$$q_\pi(B)=\Pr(\mathrm{Acc}_\pi=1\ \land\ C_\pi\le B).$$

Token and elapsed-time ceilings add separate conditions in their own units. The charge covers generation, grading, failed attempts, discarded work, and required cleanup, with unknown charges counted as outstanding liabilities. Observed cost per accepted task divides the total charge for all initiated trials by their accepted count; its population counterpart is $C_{\text{eff}}$ from @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task, with $\mathbb{E}[C_\pi]$ as the attempt cost and $\Pr(\mathrm{Acc}_\pi=1)$ as $p_{\text{acc}}$. Because failed trials are charged to accepted ones, the ratio never falls below the mean cost of the successful trials alone, and a cohort with no accepted tasks reports its spend and the zero count.

Consider a restricted comparison with independent, isolated candidates, constant pass probability $p>0$, generation cost $g$, checking cost $v$, and a checker that decides the stipulated criterion exactly. All costs are in dollars. A selector that returns the first passing candidate reaches availability $q_k=1-(1-p)^k$. Generating and checking all $k$ candidates costs $k(g+v)$. Generating and checking sequentially, stopping at the first pass or after $k$ failures, starts an expected

$$\mathbb{E}[N_k]=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-p)^j=\frac{q_k}{p}$$

candidates. The all-fail path still starts exactly $k$, so the policy is bounded. Consequently,

$$C_{\text{eff,batch}}=\frac{k(g+v)}{q_k},\qquad
C_{\text{eff,seq}}=\frac{g+v}{p}.$$ {#eq-cost-per-accepted-task-iid}
